input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-499: Computer Science Undergraduate Co-op. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: Students perform professional work related to Computer Science. Students must complete a student co-op work report for each term for which they are registered; students are also evaluated each term by their supervisor. A satisfactory grade is given for co-op when both a completed student co-op work report and a completed, corresponding supervisor evaluation are received and when both documents are generally consistent. When registered for co-op, students are considered by RIT to have full-time status. In order to register for co-op for either fall or spring semester, we expect that students will work a minimum of 14 weeks and work a minimum of 35 hours per week. Prerequisite: CSCI-099 or equivalent course. Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-499]
Students perform professional work related to Computer Science. Students must complete a student co-op work report for each term for which they are registered; students are also evaluated each term by their supervisor. A satisfactory grade is given for co-op when both a completed student co-op work report and a completed, corresponding supervisor evaluation are received and when both documents are generally consistent. When registered for co-op, students are considered by RIT to have full-time status. In order to register for co-op for either fall or spring semester, we expect that students will work a minimum of 14 weeks and work a minimum of 35 hours per week. Prerequisite: CSCI-099 or equivalent course. Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

beats.claim: Students registered for the co-op program are considered to have full-time status by the institution.
beats.example: A student enrolled in CSCI-499 for the fall semester is counted as a full-time undergraduate for financial aid and housing purposes.
beats.title: Program Overview and Status
beats.visualDirection: Display a simple badge graphic labeled 'Full-Time Status' next to a calendar showing a 14-week span.

beats.claim: Students must work a minimum of 14 weeks and 35 hours per week to register for the co-op.
beats.example: A student planning a spring co-op must schedule at least 490 hours of work spread across the semester.
beats.title: Time Commitment Requirements
beats.visualDirection: Show a bar chart comparing a 14-week minimum schedule against a 12-week schedule, highlighting the 35-hour weekly threshold.

beats.claim: Students must complete CSCI-099 or an equivalent course before registering for the co-op.
beats.example: A student who has not taken CSCI-099 must enroll in it first to become eligible for the co-op program.
beats.title: Prerequisite Coursework
beats.visualDirection: Create a linear prerequisite flowchart: 'CSCI-099' -> 'Eligible for CSCI-499 Co-op'.

beats.claim: Students must complete a student co-op work report for each term they are registered for.
beats.example: A student working on a software development project must submit a written report detailing their tasks, challenges, and outcomes.
beats.title: Student Work Report Requirement
beats.visualDirection: Show a document template with sections for 'Project Description', 'Technical Implementation', and 'Learning Outcomes'.

beats.claim: Students are evaluated each term by their supervisor, and the evaluation must correspond to the student's work.
beats.example: A supervisor reviews the student's code commits and deliverables to provide a formal performance evaluation.
beats.title: Supervisor Evaluation Requirement
beats.visualDirection: Display a two-column comparison: 'Student Report' vs. 'Supervisor Evaluation' with a checkmark indicating consistency.

beats.claim: A satisfactory grade is awarded only when both documents are generally consistent and complete.
beats.example: If the student report describes a database migration but the supervisor evaluation focuses solely on UI testing, the grade is not satisfactory.
beats.title: Grading Consistency Standard
beats.visualDirection: Use a Venn diagram showing the overlap between 'Student Report Content' and 'Supervisor Evaluation Content' as the grading zone.

beats.claim: Computing professionals must avoid harm, be honest, and strive for high quality in processes and products.
beats.example: A co-op student developing an AI model must audit training data for bias and document limitations to prevent harmful outcomes.
beats.title: Ethical Computing Principles
beats.visualDirection: Present a checklist graphic with icons for 'Avoid Harm', 'Honesty', 'High Quality', and 'Respect Privacy'.

beats.claim: Technical communication must distinguish claims from evidence, cite prior work, and avoid fabrication or falsification.
beats.example: A student's co-op report must include a literature review section that cites existing algorithms before presenting new results.
beats.title: Responsible Research Communication
beats.visualDirection: Show a side-by-side comparison of a 'Misleading Claim' (highlighted in red) versus a 'Responsible Claim' (highlighted in green) with citations.

beats.claim: Authors should preserve research integrity by making limitations and threats to validity visible and disclosing conflicts.
beats.example: A co-op project report must include a dedicated section listing data collection constraints and potential biases in the experimental setup.
beats.title: Research Integrity and Transparency
beats.visualDirection: Create a template slide with a 'Limitations & Threats' box and a 'Conflicts Disclosure' field to be filled by students.

beats.claim: Students must verify registration eligibility, document consistency, ethical compliance, and research transparency before submitting co-op materials.
beats.example: Before final submission, a student checks that their 14-week schedule is logged, their report matches the supervisor's evaluation, and all ethical guidelines are met.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a final checklist graphic with four checkboxes: '14-Week/35-Hr Commitment', 'Report-Evaluation Consistency', 'Ethical Compliance', 'Research Transparency'.

learningObjectives: Students will define the minimum time commitment and registration requirements for the co-op program.
Students will articulate the dual-document grading system and consistency standards for co-op evaluation.
Students will apply ACM ethical principles and responsible research practices to professional co-op work.
